components.name: Collapsible
components.description: One trigger and one panel. The standalone disclosure — show more, an advanced section at the foot of a form, a filter bar that folds away.
components.when_to_use: A single region worth hiding by default and cheap to open: extra fields under a summary, advanced options, a filter panel above a register, an audit trail nobody reads. The moment there are two or more of these stacked and their headings read as a set, it is an accordion — that component owns the group, the single-open rule and the heading outline, and a row of separate collapsibles pretending to be one is the thing it exists to stop. Repetition on its own does not make it an accordion, though: one disclosure per record, down a register or a table, is this component rendered in a loop, and what belongs to the accordion is a fixed set of sections on a single screen whose headings read as an outline of it. Never collapse something the user has to act on to finish the task in front of them.
rules: x-collapse comes from the Alpine collapse plugin, and the plugin has to be on the page before Alpine core. Without it the directive is not an error — it is ignored, and the panel toggles with the plain x-show underneath it, which snaps instead of animating. The failure looks like a styling problem and it is a script tag.

Never put padding or a border on the element x-collapse animates. box-sizing is border-box, so height:0 cannot go below padding-top + padding-bottom + the borders — the panel bottoms out at that height and x-show then removes it in one frame, which reads as a snap at the end of a smooth close. Padding, borders and background go on an inner div; the animated element carries nothing but the directive and its id.

That inner div takes padding, not margin. A margin on the first or last child collapses straight through the animated wrapper, so the height the plugin measures is short by the margin and the panel clips its own content until the next toggle.

A trigger inside a <form> needs type="button". The default is submit, so the first click on Advanced options posts a half-filled order instead of opening anything, and the bug only shows up once the collapsible is dropped into a real form.

The trigger goes above the panel and has a fixed height. Below the panel it is pushed down by the whole height of what just opened and the second click lands in the middle of the new content; growing when open it moves under a stationary cursor. h-9 or h-12 on the trigger and it stays where it was clicked.

The rotation binds to a wrapping <span>, never to the <i data-lucide>. createIcons() replaces that element with an <svg> and every binding on it dies with it. The span is flex because a transform needs a block-level box in Tailwind v4.

aria-expanded on the trigger, aria-controls carrying the panel id, and the panel actually carrying that id. Two out of three is the usual state of this component in the wild and it announces a button that expands nothing. When there is no panel in the DOM at all — a locked section — drop aria-controls rather than pointing it at an id that does not exist.

x-cloak on a panel that starts closed, and never on one that starts open. Alpine boots after the HTML paints: without it a closed panel is on screen for the first frames, and with it an open panel stays hidden until the script lands.

<details> and x-collapse do not combine. The browser owns the open attribute and drops the content to display:none the instant it changes, so there is no frame left to animate a height in and the two fight over the same element. Pick one: <details> for a panel that needs no script, Alpine for one that animates or is driven from elsewhere.

A collapsed panel is not a permission boundary. x-show renders the markup and hides it, so a cost breakup behind a trigger is in the page source of every user who can load the page. Gate it in the view — do not render what this user may not read.

A collapsed panel still submits. display:none inputs post exactly like visible ones, so anything typed into an advanced section and then folded away still reaches the server. That is usually what you want; it stops being what you want the moment the trigger is used to mean "these settings do not apply".

The closed state has to say what is inside it. A trigger reading Filters over a register showing 218 of 1,438 rows is how someone reports a missing order that was never missing — put the count of active filters on the trigger, or keep the applied chips outside the panel where folding it cannot hide them.

Find-in-page does not reach an x-show panel. Ctrl-F walks rendered text, and display:none is not rendered, so a term inside a closed Alpine panel simply does not exist as far as the browser is concerned. Chrome and Safari do open a closed <details> to reveal a match — which is the argument for the native variant, or for the findable one, whenever the panel holds reference text someone will search.

x-show writes display inline, so a plain class cannot override it. A panel that has to be open at md and up needs the important modifier — md:block!, with the bang at the end in Tailwind v4 — and that instance drops x-collapse, because the plugin writes an inline height too and the panel would sit at 0 on desktop.
One x-data for the pair. A trigger with its own x-data and a panel with another are two independent copies of open that never see each other; the state belongs on the nearest ancestor of both.

x-collapse writes its transition inline, and an inline style beats a class, so motion-reduce:transition-none on the panel does nothing at all. It has to be motion-reduce:transition-none! — the bang at the end, the same important modifier md:block! needs and for the same reason. The plugin still waits out its own duration and still finishes at height auto; only the interpolation goes, and the panel arrives at full height in one frame. The chevron takes the plain class, because that transition is one of ours.

hidden="until-found" is the third answer to find-in-page, between <details> and giving up on it. The browser hides the panel with content-visibility instead of display, so the text inside it is still found, and fires beforematch just before revealing it — which is where aria-expanded is put back in step. It cannot be combined with x-show, which writes display:none straight over the top of it. content-visibility keeps the element's own box, so the no-padding rule bites here too, and a browser that has not implemented it treats the attribute as a plain hidden and loses nothing but the reveal.

There is one exception to the trigger going above the panel: the tail of a list whose head is already on screen. There it has to sit under the last visible row, or it is a button promising rows the eye cannot follow to — and the price is that closing moves it. Scroll it back once the collapse has finished, with block: 'nearest' so a trigger that never left the window is left where it is.

A panel fetched on first open keeps x-show and never x-if. x-show leaves the response in the document when the panel closes, so the second open costs nothing; x-if removes it, and with hx-trigger="click once" already spent there is no second request to fill it again. A panel the server renders open never receives that first click — that instance swaps click once for load, or for intersect once on the panel body, since a display:none element never intersects.

A fetch that failed behind a closed panel is invisible. Shut, a panel that could not load is indistinguishable from one nobody has opened, and the report that comes back is that the audit trail is empty. The failure goes on the trigger, the retry goes in the panel, and the retry carries its own hx-get because the trigger has spent its one.

A panel that opens itself because something inside it needs attention reopens on $watch, never on x-effect. x-effect re-runs on every dependency it touches, so a section closed on purpose springs open again the next time any state on the page moves — the user closes it, types in the field above it, and it is back. Watch the list of failures instead: it is replaced once per validation run, which is exactly how often reopening is warranted.

In a table the pair goes in a <tbody> of its own, one per record. A table accepts any number of them and it is the only element that can hold a summary row and its detail row together — a div in that position is reparented out of the table by the parser. Drop x-collapse there as well: a row's height is settled by the table's own layout pass, so the plugin has nothing steady to animate and the row snaps regardless.

Seed the trigger label rather than leaving the x-text span empty. x-text overwrites whatever is inside the element, so Show more reads correctly on the first paint and the button is not a blank strip until Alpine boots.

anatomy.description: One x-data holding open, on the nearest element that contains both the trigger and the panel.
A real button at a fixed height, above the panel, carrying type="button", aria-expanded and aria-controls.
What the closed row still says — a count, an amount, how many filters are on. Without it the trigger is a door with nothing written on it.
A chevron in a flex span, rotated by a class on the span. Optional when the trigger label already flips between Show and Hide — two indicators say the same thing twice.

The element x-collapse animates. It carries the id, x-show, x-cloak and at most one class — motion-reduce:transition-none!, the only thing that beats the transition the plugin writes inline. No padding, no border, no background.
The inner div holding the padding, the divider and the content, so the panel can genuinely reach height 0.

behaviour: The trigger toggles one panel and nothing else. There is no group, no single-open rule and no coordination with anything beside it — that is the accordion.

The trigger does not move between states. Its height is fixed and it sits above the panel, so a second click lands on the same control the first one did. The tail of a list is the exception, and it pays for it: the trigger sits below the panel and closing has to scroll it back into view.
The panel animates its height over 200ms and finishes at height auto, so content that arrives afterwards — an htmx swap, a row added — reflows instead of being clipped.
A panel that starts closed carries x-cloak; one that starts open must not. The default state is a decision about what this record is for, not a habit.
Fields inside a collapsed panel are still in the form and still post. Closing the section hides it; it does not clear it.
A locked section shows its trigger disabled with a reason beside it, and its content is not in the document at all.
Under prefers-reduced-motion the panel arrives at its full height in one frame. The state, the timing and the closing height auto are unchanged; the interpolation is the only thing that goes.
A panel that opens itself does so once per reason. It opens when the reason arrives — a rejected field, a check that failed — and someone who closes it afterwards keeps it closed until the next one.
A panel whose content is fetched fetches once. Closing it does not discard what came back and opening it again does not ask a second time, and a fetch that failed says so on the closed trigger.
A section with nothing in it is not a collapsible. Render the one line that says so, rather than a control that opens onto nothing.
accessibility: The trigger is a button, never a div with a click handler, and inside a form it is type="button".
aria-expanded is bound to the state, not written once. aria-controls names the panel id, and the panel carries it.
Panel ids are unique on the page. Rendered in a loop they take the record key — col-lines-1187 — or the second trigger points at the first panel and both rows open the same thing.
An icon-only trigger is named for what it opens — "GST breakup" — not for what it does. Expand is what the aria-expanded state already says.
The chevron is decorative and carries no label. The trigger text is the accessible name.
<summary> is already exposed as a button with an expanded state. Adding role, aria-expanded or aria-controls to it overwrites something the browser keeps correct for free.

A count or a failure tally on the trigger joins its accessible name — "Tax and receipt settings, 2 to fix" — and that is correct. It is a fact about the section rather than instructions for working the control, and on the closed row it is the only thing there is to say.

A panel hidden with hidden="until-found" is opened by the browser and not by the trigger. Handle beforematch and set the state there, or find-in-page reveals a panel whose trigger still reports aria-expanded="false".
A disabled trigger uses the disabled attribute, so it leaves the Tab order, and the reason it is locked is text beside it rather than a title attribute.

components.name: Command palette
components.description: A ⌘K overlay for jumping to a record or firing an action by typing. It is a shortcut over the navigation, never the only route to something.
components.when_to_use: Consoles a person lives in all day with many destinations and records. Skip it on a three-page app — nobody will learn the shortcut.
rules: Everything reachable here must also be reachable by clicking. The palette is an accelerator, not a hiding place.
Both ⌘K and Ctrl-K must work, and both need .prevent — the browser binds ⌘K to the address bar.
x-cloak on the overlay, otherwise it paints over the page on first load.

A palette is a combobox, not a menu, because it has a text box. A menu moves real focus between its items; a combobox keeps real focus in the input and points at the active row with aria-activedescendant. So the rows are not buttons and not links: nothing inside role="option" may be focusable, and a row that is a tab stop puts the caret outside the search box the moment somebody presses Tab.

Because a row cannot be a link, the palette has no middle-click, no open-in-a-new-tab and no status bar saying where the row goes. The handler navigates, and a handler is not a link — which is one more reason every destination in here has to exist as a real anchor on a real page. Ship the palette as the only route to a screen and that screen cannot be bookmarked, opened in a second tab, or reached by anybody who does not know it is there.

The palette is a dialog as well as a combobox. It covers the page with a dimmed overlay, so it takes role="dialog", aria-modal="true" and a name, and it has to hold focus to earn them: aria-modal on a panel Tab can walk out of tells a screen reader the page behind is inert while the keyboard proves it is not. The two go in together or neither does.

x-trap.noscroll on the overlay does the focusing, the returning and the scroll lock, so show() sets three fields and focuses nothing itself. The trap opens on [autofocus], which is why the query input carries one: without it the trap lands on the first tabbable node, which is the Esc button. Do not also focus by hand. x-show has not written display when $nextTick runs, so focus() on the input is a silent no-op, and a bare requestAnimationFrame beats Alpine's flush, so a hand-rolled call would be racing the trap for the same element and losing on its own terms.

The row id is derived from the record — :id="'cp-' + o.id" — never from the loop index, because filtering renumbers the rows and aria-activedescendant then names whichever record moved into that slot. Key the loop on the same field or Alpine reuses nodes and the id and the row drift apart. The prefix belongs to the palette, so a second one on the page needs a second prefix or both write the same ids.

Closing returns focus to whatever opened the palette, which is not always the trigger — ⌘K fires from wherever the caret already was. x-trap captures document.activeElement when it activates and puts it back on close, so this needs no bookkeeping of its own. Without that, every dismissal drops a keyboard user at the top of the document.
The letters on the action rows are the application's own shortcuts, shown so people learn them. The palette does not listen for them, and must not: inside a search box, N types an N.

What the palette shows at rest is not the catalogue with no filter applied. Every open starts on the empty query, so that state is where the palette spends most of its life, and 1,284 orders in recency order is a list nobody reads and a first keystroke that looks like a reset. It is a short set somebody chose: the last few records this person opened and the handful of actions their role fires. The first of them is already highlighted, because ⌘K then Enter to reopen what you were last in is the single most common thing anybody does with a palette.

Where results are ranked into one list rather than split into groups by kind, the kind has to ride on each row as a word. PO-24-1187, GRN-1187 and VEN-1187 are three records to three different screens, and an icon is not enough to separate them: a 16px document glyph is the same glyph for an order and an invoice, and it is not an accessible name either.

Ranking sorts, and a sort needs a tiebreak that is not the score. Rows scoring the same have to keep the order they were in, or two keystrokes that match equally well swap the rows under the pointer and Enter takes a record nobody chose.

A row this account may not fire keeps its place in the list, greyed, with the reason under it. aria-disabled announces and blocks nothing, so the arrow keys have to step over it, the pointer must not highlight it, and the click handler has to return early. Hiding it instead means somebody searches for the same thing again next week, and it makes the list a different shape for every role.
The reason a row is unavailable is grey, not red. Red says a record is overdue or a request failed; an approval limit that has always applied is neither.

An action that needs an argument opens a second step rather than firing. The row says so by ending in an ellipsis, choosing it clears the query and puts a chip in the box naming what was already chosen, and Backspace on an empty query goes back a step — as does the first Escape, which is why Escape here pops rather than closes until there is nothing left to pop.

A prefix character narrows the palette to one kind — > actions, # records, @ people — and only at position 0, so a query with a hash in the middle of it is still a search for that text. The character stays in the box as typed text rather than being lifted into state, so there is one source of truth for the mode and Backspace is what leaves it. The prefix alone, with nothing after it, lists the whole of that kind: that is how anybody finds out what the mode holds.

Records are searched on the server; actions are not. Filtering a dozen strings the template already holds does not need a round trip, and an action list that arrives late is an action list that is missing at the moment somebody types three letters and presses Enter. So the two halves of the list come from two places, and the keyboard reads the rows out of the DOM rather than out of an array, because htmx replaced half of them without telling Alpine.

One highlight mechanism, not two. Where part of the list is swapped in by htmx, the tint is painted by one function over whatever role="option" elements are in the DOM — the Alpine-rendered rows included. A :class binding on the Alpine half and classList on the server half is two implementations of one state, and they drift apart on the first keystroke that lands mid-request.

Below sm there is no ⌘K, no Escape key and no pointer. The trigger has to be a real button, the way out has to be a control inside the panel, and the overlay has to be a column anchored to the top edge — a centred panel opens exactly where the software keyboard is about to be.

The palette is included once, by the shell. Two copies on one page is two ⌘K handlers racing, two overlays, two focus traps and two sets of row ids, and the second set silently wins every getElementById the first one does.

An action that changes something is a POST. A palette row that navigates to a GET which mutates is fired by anything that follows links — a prefetcher, a preview, somebody restoring their tabs — so the row submits a hidden form carrying the CSRF token instead.

anatomy.description: A dimmed field with the panel near the top, not centred — the list grows downward. It carries x-trap.noscroll, so it is what holds focus and locks the page behind.
role="combobox", focused on open and holding real focus the whole time the palette is up. The query is cleared on close so the next open starts fresh.
Results split by kind — actions, records — each under a small label. role="group" named by that label, and a group with no matches leaves with its heading.
One row, role="option" and not a tab stop, with the active one tinted. The keyboard drives which is active.
The word on a row saying what sort of record it is — order, receipt, vendor, item. It rides on the row wherever the results are one ranked list, because there is no heading above the row to say it.

What sits in the box on the second step of an action that needs one more thing. It names what was already chosen, is aria-hidden because the input's own label and the listbox name carry it, and Backspace on an empty query is what removes it.
What the list shows at zero matches — the query quoted back, not an empty panel.
What the empty state offers instead of a dead end: the searches the palette cannot run itself, drawn as ordinary role="option" rows so Enter still leads somewhere.
A sr-only role="status" inside the dialog, carrying the number of matches. It sits inside because aria-modal hides everything outside the dialog from a screen reader.
The key legend. Nobody learns arrow keys and Enter from nothing — and where the palette has prefix modes, this is where they are written down.

behaviour: Everything reachable here is also reachable by clicking. The palette is an accelerator, never a hiding place.
Both Cmd-K and Ctrl-K open it, and both need .prevent — the browser binds Cmd-K to the address bar.
Opening moves focus into the query input, and Tab stays inside the panel, so nothing behind the overlay is reachable until it closes.

An empty query shows the last records this person opened and the actions their role uses, not the unfiltered catalogue, and the first row is already highlighted so ⌘K then Enter reopens the last record.
Typing filters both groups at once, and every keystroke puts the highlight back on the first match, so Enter always takes the row at the top of the list.
Where the results are one ranked list rather than groups, every row says which kind of record it is, because the same number is an order, a receipt and a vendor code.

Arrow down and up move the active row over the flattened list in the order the rows are drawn, not group by group, and clamp at both ends rather than wrapping. Enter takes the active row, Escape closes.
The highlight follows the mouse as well as the keyboard, so the row under the pointer and the row Enter would take are never two different rows.
A row this account may not fire stays in the list with the reason under it, and neither the keyboard nor the pointer will put the highlight on it.
A group whose rows are all filtered out goes with its heading, and when nothing matches at all the list is replaced by an empty state naming the query.
Nothing matched leaves rows behind rather than an empty panel: the searches the palette cannot run itself are offered as options, so Enter always leads somewhere.

A row whose label ends in an ellipsis asks for something before it fires. Choosing it clears the query, puts a chip in the box naming what was chosen, and shows the second list. Backspace on an empty query goes back one step, and so does the first Escape.

A first character of >, # or @ narrows the palette to actions, records or people. The character stays in the box, so deleting it is what leaves the mode, and the character on its own lists the whole of that kind.

Records are searched on the server on a debounced query with a two-character floor, while the actions are matched in the browser. Below the floor the record rows are cleared, so last search's answer never sits under a query that did not produce it.

Below sm the overlay is the screen: no scrim, the box at the top edge where the keyboard cannot cover it, the list scrolling in what is left, and a Cancel control in the panel because there is no Escape key to press.
Closing clears the query, so reopening does not present the previous search as if it were current, and puts focus back on whatever opened the palette.
On a three-page application, skip it entirely — nobody will learn the shortcut.
accessibility: The input is role="combobox" with aria-autocomplete="list", aria-expanded, aria-controls naming the list and aria-activedescendant naming the active row.

The list is role="listbox" with an accessible name and every row is role="option". No row carries aria-selected: a palette commits nothing — a row is fired and the palette closes — so the only state a row has is being the active one, and aria-activedescendant is what carries that.
Real focus never leaves the input. The highlight moves through aria-activedescendant, which is why every row needs a stable id derived from the record and why no row is a tab stop.

A row is never an anchor or a button. Nothing inside role="option" may be focusable, so the row is a div and the navigation happens in the handler — which is a real cost, and the reason the same destination has to be a real link somewhere else.

Each group is role="group" named by its heading, and the visible heading is aria-hidden — the group is already named, and a bare paragraph is not a permitted child of a listbox. A container that is only there to be a swap target takes role="none", which drops it out of the tree and leaves its options exposed to the group above.

A disabled row keeps aria-disabled="true" and keeps its place. aria-disabled is an announcement and not a behaviour: the arrow keys, the pointer and the click handler each have to honour it separately.

The number of matches is announced from a role="status" inside the dialog. Outside it the announcement would never arrive, because aria-modal="true" takes everything outside the dialog out of the accessibility tree.

When the palette changes step or mode, the input's accessible name and the listbox name change with it and the status says which step it is on. The chip drawn in the box is aria-hidden, because those two already carry it and a third copy is read out as loose text beside the field.
The overlay is role="dialog" with aria-modal="true", named "Command palette", so the rest of the page is out of the accessibility tree while it is open.
The trigger carries aria-haspopup="dialog", and any ⌘K hint drawn inside it is aria-hidden — it is a reminder of the shortcut, not part of the button's name.
Focus is trapped in the panel and cannot reach the page behind. The trap opens on the query input because it carries autofocus, rather than on the Esc button, which is the first tabbable node.

Escape closes and returns focus to whatever opened the palette, captured by x-trap at the moment it activated. Where the palette has steps, the first Escape pops the step and only the last one closes.

variants.name: Rendered by the shell, filtered by permission
variants.html:
{% comment %} templates/_command_palette.html — included once, by the shell, never by a page. Two copies is two ⌘K handlers racing for the same keystroke, two overlays, two focus traps, and two sets of row ids where the second silently wins every getElementById the first one does. The prose is {% comment %} and not {# #}. A hash comment is single-line only — the tokeniser matches it without DOTALL — so a block like this one written that way is not a comment at all, it is text, and every tag inside it renders. That includes the include below, which would render this template inside itself. base.html, inside the app shell {% include '_command_palette.html' %} The action list is built in the view and not in the template. An {% if perms %} around each row inside x-data would work, but it puts the permission rules in an HTML attribute where nobody auditing permissions will look, and the same list has to drive the menu that this palette accelerates. One function, two consumers. views.py / palette.py def palette_actions(user): out = [] if user.has_perm('purchasing.add_purchaseorder'): out.append({'id': 'new-po', 'label': 'New purchase order', 'icon': 'plus', 'url': reverse('order-new')}) if user.has_perm('stores.add_goodsreceipt'): out.append({'id': 'post-grn', 'label': 'Post goods receipt', 'icon': 'package-check', 'url': reverse('grn-new')}) if user.has_perm('purchasing.approve_purchaseorder'): out.append({'id': 'approvals', 'label': 'Go to my approvals', 'icon': 'check-check', 'url': reverse('approvals')}) # a POST, because it changes something. See the form below. out.append({'id': 'resync', 'label': 'Resync the vendor master', 'icon': 'refresh-cw', 'url': reverse('vendor-resync'), 'method': 'post'}) return out context_processors.py — the palette is on every page, so its data is on every context. Anything more expensive than these two queries belongs behind the htmx variant instead of in a context processor. def palette(request): if not request.user.is_authenticated: return {} return {'palette_actions': palette_actions(request.user), 'palette_recents': recent_for(request.user)[:5]} Both lists go through json_script. Never interpolate a queryset into an x-data attribute: one vendor called M/s D'Souza Traders ends the attribute early and the component stops parsing. json_script escapes for exactly that. recent_for(user) returns the same shape the rows are drawn from — id, label, sub, amount, icon and url — because the row id is 'cpd-' + o.id and aria-activedescendant is going to point at it. A row that a permission check dropped must be dropped from the menu as well. A palette that lists an action the view refuses is a 403 with extra steps, and a palette that hides one the menu still shows teaches people to distrust it. {% endcomment %} {{ palette_actions|json_script:"cpd-actions" }} {{ palette_recents|json_script:"cpd-recents" }}
{% comment %} An action that changes something is a POST. A row that navigates to a GET which mutates is fired by anything that follows links — a prefetcher, a link preview, a browser restoring tabs — and the palette is a place where one keystroke follows a link. {% endcomment %}
